K.A.W.Williams }} '''''Brachychiton rupestris''''' ([[common name|commonly]] known as the '''narrow-leaved bottle tree''' or '''Queensland bottle tree''') is a [[tree]] in the family [[Malvaceae]],{{efn|1=The genus ''Brachychiton'' was traditionally placed in the family [[Sterculiaceae]], but that family, along with [[Bombacaceae]] and [[Tiliaceae]], has been found to be [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]] and is now sunk into a more broadly-defined [[Malvaceae]]{{cite web|url=http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/research/APweb/|title=Angiosperm Phylogeny Website|last=Stevens|first=Peter F.|author-link=Peter F. Stevens|date=29 January 2015|access-date=6 February 2015}}}} [[Endemism|endemic]] to the Australian state of [[Queensland]]. [[Species description|Described]] by Sir [[Thomas Mitchell (explorer)|Thomas Mitchell]] and [[John Lindley]] in 1848, it earned its name from its bulbous [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]], which can be up to {{convert|3.5|m|ft}} in [[diameter at breast height]] (DBH). Reaching around {{convert|10|–|25|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, the Queensland bottle tree is [[deciduous]], losing its leaves seasonally, between September and December. The [[Leaf|leaves]] are simple or divided, with one or more narrow [[leaf blade]]s up to {{convert|11|cm|in|sigfig=1}} long and {{convert|2|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide. Cream-coloured [[flower]]s appear from September to November, and are followed by woody, boat-shaped [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] that [[Fruit ripening|ripen]] from November to May. No subspecies are recognised. As a [[drought deciduous]] and [[Succulent plant|succulent]] tree, much like the [[Adansonia|baobab]] (''Adansonia'') of [[Madagascar]], ''B. rupestris'' adapts readily to cultivation, and is quite tolerant of a range of soils and temperatures. It is a key component and [[Rainforest#Emergent layer|emergent]] tree in the endangered central semi-evergreen vine thickets (also known as bottletree scrub) of the Queensland [[Brigalow Belt]]. Remnant trees are often left by farmers on cleared land for their value as shade and fodder trees, and as homes for various birds and animals. ==Description== [[File:Roma's largest bottle tree.jpg|thumb|left|Largest bottle tree in Roma, Queensland, where the species is used extensively for street plantings]] ''Brachychiton rupestris'' grows as a [[Succulent plant|succulent]] tree reaching {{convert|10|–|20|m|ft|abbr=on}}, rarely {{convert|25|m|ft|abbr=on}}, in height, though plants in cultivation are usually shorter.{{cite web|author=Cheung, Puiyee |title=Brachychiton rupestris|work=Growing Native Plants|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens and Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research, Canberra.|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2005/brachychiton-rupestris.html|access-date=2 December 2014}} The thick trunk is {{convert|5|–|15|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with a {{convert|1|–|3.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[diameter at breast height]] (DBH). It has dark grey bark and is marked by shallow [[Tessellation#In nature|tessellation]] and deeper fissures. Smaller branches are light green or grey, as are the trunks of immature trees. Like those of all members of the genus, the leaves are [[phyllotaxis|alternately arranged]] along the stems. ''B. rupestris'' is [[deciduous]]. Trees in their native habitat are typically leafless between September and December; the timing, duration and extent of leaf drop may be affected by extremes of rainfall or drought. Sometimes trees shed leaves from only some branches.{{cite book|last=Kapitany|first=Attila|title=Australian Succulent Plants|publisher=Kapitany Concepts|location=Boronia, Victoria|date=2007|pages=214–16|isbn=978-0-646-46381-0}} On every tree, the leaves vary in shape, ranging from narrow and elliptic to deeply divided. The upper surface is glossy, contrasting with a pale undersurface. The adult leaf blades are {{convert|4|–|11|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.8|–|2|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide with pointed ([[wikt:acuminate|acuminate]] or [[wikt:apiculate|apiculate]]) tips. They have a raised [[wikt:midrib|midrib]] on the upper and lower surface, with 12–25 pairs of lateral veins that are more prominent on the upper surface, arising at 50–60 degrees from the midrib. The compound [[heteroblasty|juvenile leaves]] have 3–9 spear-shaped (lanceolate) or linear lobes. These each measure {{convert|4|–|14|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.3|–|1|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide. [[Panicle]]s of creamy-yellow flowers with red markings{{cite book|author=Rowell, Raymond J.| title=Ornamental Flowering Trees in Australia| publisher=AH & AW Reed Pty Ltd|location= Wellington, New Zealand | year=1980 |page=59| isbn=0-589-50178-X}} appear from September to November in the species' native range. These arise from [[axillary bud]]s on end branches. Each panicle contains 10–30 flowers and is {{convert|3|–|8|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, and each flower is {{convert|0.5|–|1|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.3|–|1.8|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide. The length of the lobes of the [[perianth]] is more than half the perianth diameter. Like all ''Brachychiton'' species, ''B. rupestris'' is [[Plant reproductive morphology#Terminology|monoecious]]—each plant has distinct male and female flowers. Male flowers have 15 [[stamen]]s, with pale yellow [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]], while female flowers have cream or white [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]] surrounded by rudimentary stellate (star-shaped) [[Gynoecium|carpels]], which sit atop the ovaries. Groups of 3 to 5 woody boat-shaped [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]], each containing 4 to 8 (or occasionally up to 12) seeds, develop from November to May. The follicles, smooth on the outer surface and hairy inside, split along their length to reveal seeds. The seeds, which are ovoid with a smooth surface, and {{convert|6|–|7|mm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|3.5|–|4.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide, are covered by a hairy coating known as the [[Seed#Seed coat 2|exotesta]]. The closely related Proserpine bottle tree (''[[Brachychiton compactus]]'') that occurs only in the vicinity of the town of [[Proserpine, Queensland|Proserpine]] can be distinguished by its more oval leaves, more compact flower heads, and longer ellipsoid follicles.{{sfn|Rathie|2014|p=24}} The [[Species description|undescribed]] Ormeau bottle tree has brighter lime-green new foliage and leaves but is otherwise similar to the Proserpine bottle tree.{{sfn|Rathie|2014|p=26}} ==Taxonomy and naming== {{Multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | header = Leaves | width = | image1 = Brachychiton rupestris juvenile leaf 4167.jpg | alt1 = | caption1 = Juvenile | image2 = Brachychiton rupestris adult leaves 4209.jpg | alt2 = | caption2 = Adult }} The species came to the attention of the scientific community when explorer [[Thomas Mitchell (explorer)|Sir Thomas Mitchell]] observed the trees on his expedition through Queensland in 1848 and published an account in ''Journal of an Expedition into the Interior of Tropical Australia'' in the same year. He came across them as he ascended [[Mount Abundance, Queensland|Mount Abundance]] near present-day [[Roma, Queensland|Roma]], remarking that "The trunk bulged out in the middle like a barrel, to nearly twice the diameter at the ground, or of that at the first springing of the branches above. These were small in proportion to their great girth, and the whole tree looked very odd."{{cite book|author=Mitchell, Thomas Livingstone |title=Journal of an Expedition into the Interior of Tropical Australia, in Search of a Route from Sydney to the Gulf of Carpentaria|pages=153–55|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GMoNAAAAQAAJ|year=1848|publisher=Longman, Brown, Green and Longmans}} In the same publication, English botanist [[John Lindley]] provided the first formal [[Species description|description]].{{APNI |id=30316 |title=''Delabechea rupestris'' |access-date=1 December 2014 }} Lindley placed it in the genus ''Delabechea'' as the sole representative—''Delabechea rupestris''.{{cite journal|last=Guymer|first=Gordon Paul|date=1988|title=A taxonomic revision of ''Brachychiton'' (Sterculiaceae)|journal=Australian Systematic Botany|volume=1|issue=3|pages=199–323 [243–45] | doi=10.1071/SB9880199 |bibcode=1988AuSyB...1..199G }} The genus name was selected by Mitchell to honour the director of the [[British Geological Survey]], [[Henry De la Beche]], while the Latin [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''rupestris'' (meaning 'living among rocks') alludes to the rocky hilltop habitat of specimens observed by Mitchell.{{cite journal|last=Horton|journal=Annals of Horticulture|title = Curiosities of Vegetation: The Bottle Tree of Australia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tF8CAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA154|year=1850|pages=154–56}} Ferdinand von Mueller, the Government Botanist in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], renamed it ''Brachychiton delabechei'' in 1862,{{cite book|last=Von Mueller|first=Ferdinand|title=The Plants Indigenous to the Colony of Victoria|publisher=John Ferres, Government Printer|date=1862|volume=1|page=157|url=https://archive.org/stream/plantsindigenou00muelgoog#page/n202/mode/2up}} incorporating the genus ''Delabechea'' into ''Brachychiton''. In his landmark ''[[Flora Australiensis]]'', English botanist [[George Bentham]] published the first key for the nine described species of ''Brachychiton'', and relegated them to a section of ''[[Sterculia]]''. Hence the Queensland bottle tree became ''Sterculia rupestris''.{{cite encyclopedia | last = Bentham | first = George | author-link = George Bentham | year = 1863 | title = Sterculia | encyclopedia = Flora Australiensis: Volume 1: Ranunculaceae to Anacardiaceae | volume = 1 | page = 230 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/6721350 | location = London, United Kingdom| publisher = L. Reeve & Co}} Von Mueller maintained his recognition of ''Brachychiton'' as a separate genus. German botanist [[Otto Kuntze]] challenged the generic name ''Sterculia'' in 1891, on the grounds that the name ''Clompanus'' took precedence. He republished the Queensland bottle tree as ''Clompanus rupestris''.{{cite book|last=Kuntze|first=Otto|author-link=Otto Kuntze|title=Revisio generum plantarum:vascularium omnium atque cellularium multarum secundum leges nomenclaturae internationales cum enumeratione plantarum exoticarum in itinere mundi collectarum|publisher=A. Felix|location=Leipzig, Germany|year=1891|volume=1 |page=78 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/127537}} German botanist [[Karl Moritz Schumann]] gave it its current [[binomial name]] in 1893,{{cite journal|last=Schumann|first=Karl Moritz|date=1893|title=Brachychiton|journal=Die Natürlichen Pflanzenfamilien|volume=3|issue=6|page=96|language=de|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/16815611}} which was accepted by Achille Terraciano of the [[Orto botanico di Palermo]]{{cite journal|last=Terraciano|first=Achille|date=1897|journal=Bollettino del R. Orto Botanico di Palermo|volume=1|pages=50–64 [64] |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40739088 |title=Le Specie del Genere ''Brachychiton''|language=it}} and subsequent authorities, and remains current. In 1988, [[Gordon P. Guymer|Gordon Guymer]] of the [[Queensland Herbarium]] published a taxonomic revision of ''Brachychiton''; he classified ''B. rupestris'' in the [[Section (botany)|section]] ''Delabechea'' along with the related and newly described Proserpine bottle tree. A third species, from southeast Queensland, has been recognised but not yet described.{{sfn|Rathie|2014|p=26}} Unique to the section, all three species have bulbous trunks and can have large cavities in the vertical wood [[Parenchyma (botany)|parenchyma]].{{sfn|Rathie|2014|p=24}} The genus ''Brachychiton'' lies within an Australasian [[clade]] within the subfamily [[Sterculioideae]] (previously family [[Sterculiaceae]]) in a large broadly defined [[Malvaceae]]. It is only distantly related to ''Sterculia'', belonging to a different clade within the Sterculioideae.{{cite journal | title=Phylogenetic Relationships within the Subfamily Sterculioideae (Malvaceae/Sterculiaceae-Sterculieae) Using the Chloroplast Gene ''ndhF'' |author1=Wilkie, Peter |author2=Clark, Alexandra |author3=Pennington, R. Toby |author4=Cheek, Martin |author5=Bayer, Clemens |author6=Wilcock, Chris C. | journal=Systematic Botany |year=2006|volume=31|issue=1 |pages=160–70 |doi=10.1600/036364406775971714|bibcode=2006SysBo..31..160W |s2cid=85676723 }} The name of the genus is derived from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] {{Lang|grc-Latn|brachys}}, 'short', and {{Lang|grc-Latn|chiton}}, 'tunic', a reference to the loose [[seed]] coats. ''Brachychiton'' was for many years misconstrued as being of neuter gender—first by the genus describers [[Heinrich Wilhelm Schott]] and [[Stephan Endlicher]] and later by von Mueller and others—with the specific names then incorrectly amended. Thus the bottle tree's binomial was recorded as ''Brachychiton rupestre'', now regarded as an [[orthographical variant]].{{APNI |id=308282 |title=''Brachychiton rupestre'' |access-date=4 December 2014 }} Besides Queensland bottle tree, common names for the species include narrow-leaved bottle tree and bottle tree. ''Brachychiton'' × ''turgidulus'' is a naturally occurring hybrid cross of ''B. rupestris'' with the kurrajong ''[[Brachychiton populneus|B. populneus]]'' subsp. ''populneus''. It is particularly prevalent east of [[Boonah, Queensland|Boonah]]. ==Distribution and habitat== [[File:Brachychiton rupestris flower 4443.jpg|thumb|Female flower]] ''Brachychiton rupestris'' is found in central Queensland from latitude 22° S to 28° S, with the western limits of its range defined by the 500 mm rainfall [[isohyet]]. It grows on the tops and slopes of hills or ridges in low hilly country, in clay, shale, or basalt soils. It is an [[Rainforest#Emergent layer|emergent]] tree in forests dominated by brigalow (''[[Acacia harpophylla]]''), hoop pine (''[[Araucaria cunninghamii]]''), or ooline (''[[Cadellia pentastylis]]''). It is always present in the Central semi-evergreen vine thicket—also known as Bottletree Scrub—of the [[Brigalow Belt]]. Other common species include broad-leaved bottle tree (''[[Brachychiton australis]]'') and belah (''[[Casuarina cristata]]''). The narrow-leaved bottle tree is replaced by the [[Brachychiton populneus|kurrajong]] in similar communities in New South Wales.{{cite web|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicshowcommunity.pl?id=24|title=Semi-evergreen vine thickets of the Brigalow Belt (North and South) and Nandewar Bioregions|last=Department of the Environment|date=19 February 2014|work=Threatened Species & Ecological Communities|publisher=Commonwealth of Australia|access-date=4 December 2014}} ===Conservation=== Although the species status under Queensland's [[Nature Conservation Act 1992|Nature Conservation Act]] is [[least concern]],{{cite web|title=''Brachychiton rupestris''|work=WetlandInfo|publisher=Queensland Government|url=http://wetlandinfo.ehp.qld.gov.au/wetlands/ecology/components/species/?brachychiton-rupestris|access-date=4 December 2014}} it is an emergent tree species in an endangered ecosystem known as "semi-evergreen vine thickets of the Brigalow Belt (North and South) and Nandewar bioregions", listed under the Commonwealth [[EPBC Act]],{{cite web|title=National recovery plan for the "Semi-evergreen vine thickets of the Brigalow Belt (North and South) and Nandewar Bioregions" ecological community |publisher=Department of the Environment|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicshowcommunity.pl?id=24#status|access-date=4 December 2014}} and is declining across its range. Furthermore, the health of trees in cleared areas may be compromised. The species is conserved within its natural habitat in a number of National Parks including [[Auburn River National Park|Auburn River]],{{cite web|title=Auburn River National Park|date=19 October 2009 rupestris'' has been recorded as a host plant for the mistletoe species ''[[Dendrophthoe glabrescens]]''.{{cite journal |last=Downey |first=Paul O. |year=1998 |title=An inventory of host species for by the species include the [[Dysdercus sidae|pale cotton stainer]] bug, a pest of [[cotton]] crops, and the [[Sylepa cytalis|kurrajong leaf roller]] caterpillar that chews on the foliage and rolls |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UWifn5wT6D8C&pg=PA681|year=2002|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|isbn=978-0-643-06875-9|page=681}}{{cite web|title=Pale cotton stainers|publisher=Cotton Catchment Communities scrub is a key habitat of the near threatened [[black-breasted buttonquail]].{{cite book|last=McGowan|first=Phil|author2=Madge, Steve|title=Pheasants, Partridges & Grouse: Including buttonquails, sandgrouse and allies|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing|location=London, United Kingdom|date=2010|orig-year=2002|pages=429–30|isbn=978-1-4081-3565-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WffUBAAAQBAJ&q=brachychiton+rupestris&pg=PA429}} ''Brachychiton rupestris'' can withstand bushfires and responds by flowering and putting forth new foliage afterwards. ==Uses== Aboriginal people made use of the trees through eating the roots of young plants and by consuming secretions from the trunk that were induced by wounds.{{cite book|author=Anderson, E.R.|title=Plants of Central Queensland: Their Identification and Uses|year=2003|publisher=Department of Primary Industries|isbn=978-0-7345-0249-0}} Fibre obtained from the species was used to make nets.{{cite book|author=Thozet, A.|title=List of Some of the Roots, Tubers, Bulbs and Fruits Used as Vegetable Food by the Aboriginals of Northern Queensland, Australia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RS09AQAAIAAJ&pg=PA259|year=1867|publisher=Blundell & co., printers|page=259}} The leaves have also been used for [[fodder]], and Queensland farmers often leave bottle trees as a potential food source when land is cleared. During drought conditions, whole trees have been felled to feed stock. The soft edible pulp inside the trunk is exposed by removing the bark. The pulp is energy-rich but protein-poor, and occasional cases of [[nitrate poisoning]] have led to cattle deaths. ==Cultivation== [[File:Brachychiton rupestris fruits.jpg|thumb|Open follicles split longitudinally to reveal seeds inside. The follicle interior is lined with hairs that can irritate skin.]] Bottle trees are commonly found planted in streets and parks, on farms, and as features in gardens. An avenue in [[Roma, Queensland|Roma]], Queensland, was planted between 1918 and 1920, each tree representing one of 93 local men killed in [[World War I|World War'' ''I]].{{cite web|title=Roma War Memorial Heroes Avenue|work=Queensland War Memorial Register|date=23 June 2014|publisher=The State of Queensland (Department of Environment and Heritage Protection)|url= http://www.qldwarmemorials.com.au/memorial/?id=1056|access-date=1 December 2014}} The species has been cultivated as an [[Houseplant|indoor plant]] and a [[bonsai]] subject.{{cite book|author1=Wrigley, John W. |author2=Fagg Murray |year=1979|title=Australian Native Plants|publisher=William Collins Publishers Sydney, Australia|page=314|isbn=0-00-216416-7}}{{cite book|author=Squire, David|publisher=New Holland Publishers, Limited|title=Bonsai Bible|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w6pHM58gomoC&pg=PA145|year= 2008|isbn=978-1-84773-230-9|page=145}} Bottle trees grow best in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, in full sunshine. They are suited to cultivation in regional climates equivalent to [[hardiness zone|USDA hardiness zones]] 9 to 12.{{cite web|title=Queensland bottle tree: ''Brachychition rupestris''|work=SelecTree|publisher=Urban Forest Ecosystems Institute, California Polytechnic State University|url=http://selectree.calpoly.edu/treedetail.lasso?rid=1511|access-date=3 December 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141226095754/http://selectree.calpoly.edu/treedetail.lasso?rid=1511|archive-date=26 December 2014|df=dmy-all}} In the first stages of growth, the bottle tree is very slow-growing, and the formation of the unique bottle shape is not visible until the tree is about 5 to 8 years old.{{cite web|title=''Brachychiton rupestris''|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)|url=http://anpsa.org.au/b-rup.html|access-date=2 December 2014|archive-date=9 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140809111435/http://anpsa.org.au/b-rup.html|url-status=dead}} Mature trees transplant easily, and can withstand intervals of up to three months between digging and replanting without detriment. Bottle trees grown from seed may take up to 20 years to flower. Flowering takes place after adult leaves have appeared.{{sfn|Rathie|2014|p=196}} Plants are readily propagated from seed. As seed is surrounded by irritating hairs within the pod, extraction requires care. Stem [[cutting (plant)|cuttings]] of semi-mature growth can be taken in late summer and require the application of [[auxin|rooting hormones]] and [[Seed propagation mat|bottom heat]].{{cite book|author=Koenig, Odile|title=Encyclopédie visuelle des plantes d'intérieur|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tUT8d6_1JoIC&pg=PA125|year=2005|publisher=Editions Artemis|isbn=978-2-84416-268-7|page=125|language=fr}} ==See also== *''[[Adansonia gregorii]]'', the bottle tree or baobab of Western Australia and the Northern Territory. ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{reflist}} ===Cited text=== {{Commons category}} *{{cite book|last=Rathie|first=Kerry|title=Brachychitons: Flame Trees, Kurrajongs and Bottle Trees|publisher=self-published|location=Brisbane, Queensland|date=2014|isbn=978-0-646-92681-0}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q2662709}} [[Category:Brachychiton|rupestris]] [[Category:Flora of Queensland]] [[Category:Malvales of Australia]] [[Category:Trees of Australia]] [[Category:Ornamental trees]] [[Category:Drought-tolerant trees]] [[Category:Plants described in 1848]] [[Category:Caudiciform plants]]
